name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
purpose: Standardize how AI host applications connect to external tools, data resources, and prompt templates through unified client-server capabilities.
how_it_works: Hosts launch local stdio or remote Streamable HTTP MCP servers that exchange JSON-RPC messages for capability discovery and tool execution.
transport_and_auth: Local stdio process pipes or HTTPS Streamable HTTP with OAuth 2.1 bearer tokens and RFC 9728 discovery.
strengths: Decouples model hosts from custom tool connectors, enables dynamic discovery, and supports portable third-party tool servers.
limitations: Requires strict vetting of external server permissions and tool metadata against hidden instruction tampering.

name: Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A)
purpose: Enable independent, opaque AI agents across diverse frameworks and organizations to discover skills, exchange artifacts, and collaborate on long tasks.
how_it_works: Agents publish JSON Agent Cards describing skills and endpoints, then submit and stream lifecycle task updates between clients and remote servers.
transport_and_auth: HTTPS JSON-RPC and REST with Server-Sent Events streaming plus OpenAPI-style OAuth, JWT, and API key auth schemes.
strengths: Preserves encapsulation of internal prompts and proprietary logic while enabling cross-vendor multi-agent task handoffs.
limitations: Distributed network discovery and asynchronous multi-party authentication introduce coordination and monitoring complexity.

name: OpenAPI Specification 3.1.0
purpose: Provide a machine-readable, language-agnostic contract describing REST HTTP endpoints, parameters, response schemas, and authentication methods.
how_it_works: JSON or YAML specification documents define path operations, JSON Schema 2020-12 payloads, and security schemes parsed to generate agent tool adapters.
transport_and_auth: HTTP over TLS with API keys, HTTP bearer tokens, OAuth 2.0 flows, and OpenID Connect discovery schemes.
strengths: Ubiquitous existing enterprise tooling allows rapid exposure of documented SaaS services as typed agent actions.
limitations: Large raw REST specs often overload model context windows without curated endpoint filtering and agent-focused summaries.

name: JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12)
purpose: Declare formal validation rules, property types, required fields, enums, and patterns for JSON tool arguments and structured model outputs.
how_it_works: Schema vocabularies specify constraints validated both by decoding grammars inside model APIs and host validators prior to tool dispatch.
transport_and_auth: Transport-agnostic declarative JSON data contract embedded across API payloads, OpenAPI specs, and MCP manifests.
strengths: Enforces strict machine-checkable parameter contracts that catch malformed tool calls before side effects execute.
limitations: Deeply nested schemas and arbitrary regex constructs can fail simplified constrained decoding subsets on some model backends.

name: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework (RFC 6749)
purpose: Allow third-party applications and agent tool hosts to obtain scoped, revocable delegated access to HTTP resources without sharing raw passwords.
how_it_works: Authorization servers authenticate resource owners, present explicit scope consent, and issue time-limited bearer access and refresh tokens.
transport_and_auth: HTTPS redirects and token endpoints issuing bearer tokens over Authorization HTTP headers.
strengths: Proven global standard separating identity consent from tool hosts while limiting token lifetime and permission scope.
limitations: Legacy RFC 6749 includes weaker optional grant flows removed in OAuth 2.1 such as implicit bearer fragments.

name: OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework (Draft-17)
purpose: Consolidate modern OAuth security best practices into a unified authorization baseline required by contemporary remote agent protocols like MCP.
how_it_works: Mandates PKCE with S256 verification for authorization codes, requires exact redirect matching, and eliminates legacy implicit and password grants.
transport_and_auth: HTTPS with mandatory PKCE code challenges, exact redirect URIs, and bearer tokens carried in Authorization headers.
strengths: Hardens delegated tool authentication against interception and bearer token leakage across browser and native clients.
limitations: Remains an active IETF Internet-Draft still undergoing working group finalization into a formal RFC.

name: OpenTelemetry (OTEL)
purpose: Standardize telemetry APIs, trace context propagation, and semantic conventions across traces, metrics, and logs for AI agent pipelines.
how_it_works: Agent frameworks emit hierarchical parent-child spans annotated with standardized GenAI model, token, and tool attributes exported over OTLP.
transport_and_auth: OTLP over gRPC or HTTP/protobuf with W3C TraceContext headers and token/mTLS transport authentication.
strengths: Prevents observability vendor lock-in while correlating LLM spans cleanly alongside downstream database and microservice traces.
limitations: Rapidly evolving GenAI semantic conventions require occasional schema mapping updates across evaluation platforms.

name: OpenAI Function Calling and Responses API Contract
purpose: Provide a de facto HTTP JSON interface for chat completions, structured outputs, tool calling, streaming chunks, and stateful agent turns.
how_it_works: Clients post typed message lists and tool schemas over HTTPS JSON and parse structured tool-call deltas or SSE responses.
transport_and_auth: HTTPS JSON and Server-Sent Events using bearer API key authorization headers.
strengths: Adopted across open-source inference engines and gateways as a portable interchange target across hosted and local models.
limitations: Vendor-specific extensions such as specialized reasoning metadata or built-in server tools diverge across compatible providers.

name: Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP)
purpose: Standardize how AI agents initiate checkout flows, verify merchant pricing, and delegate scoped payment tokens without handling raw credentials.
how_it_works: Agents interact with merchant checkout APIs using structured cart schemas and cryptographic shared payment tokens bounded by merchant limits.
transport_and_auth: HTTPS JSON APIs with scoped cryptographic payment tokens and webhook verification signatures.
strengths: Maintains merchant-of-record controls and reduces fraud risk by keeping raw financial instruments out of agent contexts.
limitations: Early ecosystem adoption means merchants must build compatible checkout endpoints and webhook integrations.

name: JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519)
purpose: Represent cryptographically signed or encrypted identity, delegation, and permission claims compactly across distributed agent hops.
how_it_works: Header, payload claims, and JWS signature segments encode base64url strings verified using public JWKS keys without stateful DB lookups.
transport_and_auth: Header bearer tokens or signed assertion parameters carried over HTTPS, A2A, and OAuth requests.
strengths: Enables stateless cryptographic verification of user identity, workload principal, scopes, and short expiration windows.
limitations: Signed tokens remain valid until expiry if compromised unless combined with short TTLs or active revocation checks.

name: The WebSocket Protocol (RFC 6455)
purpose: Provide persistent full-duplex bidirectional client-server channels over a single TCP connection for low-latency realtime audio and control events.
how_it_works: An HTTP Upgrade handshake transitions into bidirectional text and binary WebSocket frames with low per-message framing overhead.
transport_and_auth: WSS over TLS with HTTP upgrade bearer tokens, query parameters, or cookie session binding.
strengths: Supports concurrent bidirectional streaming required for low-latency voice interruption and live multimodal agent feedback.
limitations: Long-lived stateful sockets complicate horizontal load balancing and proxy timeout configuration compared to stateless HTTP.

name: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
purpose: Stream incremental UTF-8 text event payloads continuously from HTTP servers to clients over standard unidirectional HTTP connections.
how_it_works: Servers respond with text/event-stream content type and flush formatted data events incrementally as LLM tokens or agent updates arrive.
transport_and_auth: Standard HTTP/HTTPS GET or POST responses using bearer token headers without separate upgrade protocols.
strengths: Works seamlessly through standard corporate proxies and HTTP load balancers with simple incremental token rendering.
limitations: Supports server-to-client streaming only, requiring separate client POST calls for interactive mid-stream interruptions.

name: OpenID Connect Core 1.0
purpose: Add a standardized verifiable user authentication and identity token layer directly atop OAuth authorization flows.
how_it_works: Authorization servers return a signed JWT ID token alongside OAuth access tokens plus standard UserInfo endpoints for user verification.
transport_and_auth: HTTPS OAuth redirects issuing signed JWS ID tokens verified against published provider JWKS metadata.
strengths: Gives enterprise agent portals unified SSO login and reliable human-principal identity bindings across downstream delegations.
limitations: Requires careful distinction between authentication ID tokens and resource-scoped access tokens when delegating tool calls.

name: OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)
purpose: Allow remote resource servers such as MCP endpoints to advertise authoritative OAuth servers, supported scopes, and capabilities dynamically.
how_it_works: Protected resources publish a well-known JSON metadata document enabling clients to discover which authorization server governs access.
transport_and_auth: HTTPS GET on well-known protected resource metadata endpoints linked via HTTP WWW-Authenticate headers.
strengths: Removes hardcoded authorization server configuration between dynamic MCP hosts and third-party remote tool providers.
limitations: Requires clients to validate discovered authorization server URLs carefully against SSRF and phishing redirects.

name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI Management System
purpose: Establish auditable organizational policies, risk assessments, human oversight processes, and continuous improvement across AI system lifecycles.
how_it_works: Organizations implement structured governance controls, risk registers, supplier checks, and internal audit loops eligible for third-party certification.
transport_and_auth: Organizational governance standard rather than wire protocol; relies on documented audit trails and identity governance.
strengths: Provides a globally recognized certifiable baseline integrating AI safety governance with enterprise quality processes.
limitations: Organizational certification overhead requires sustained documentation and executive governance beyond engineering controls alone.

name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
purpose: Guide organizations through Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions to identify and mitigate technical and sociotechnical AI risks.
how_it_works: Teams execute voluntary risk profiling—paired with the Generative AI Profile—across trustworthiness dimensions including validity, safety, privacy, and fairness.
transport_and_auth: Governance methodology mapping system risks to verification controls, access management, and lifecycle monitoring.
strengths: Offers a vendor-neutral, practical vocabulary widely adopted across US federal guidance and enterprise compliance reviews.
limitations: Voluntary guidance leaves concrete technical threshold definitions and control implementations to adopting engineering teams.
